title: The Frobenius–Schur Indicator
---

The trichotomy of Theorem [16.5.4](/notes/math-55a/16-5-quaternionic-representations#theorem-16-5-4) can be detected numerically, from the character alone.

:::definition{16.6.1} Frobenius–Schur indicator
The ***Frobenius–Schur indicator*** of a representation $V$ of $G$ is $$\nu(V) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_V(g^2).$$
:::

:::theorem{16.6.2} Frobenius–Schur
For an irreducible representation $V$ of $G$, $$\nu(V) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V \text{ is real}, \\ 0 & \text{if } \chi_V \text{ is not real-valued}, \\ -1 & \text{if } V \text{ is quaternionic}. \end{cases}$$
:::

:::proof
Let $s : V \otimes V \to V \otimes V$ be the linear map with $s(v \otimes w) = w \otimes v$. It commutes with the action of $G$ and satisfies $s^2 = \id$, so $V \otimes V = S \oplus A$, where $$S = \{x : s(x) = x\} \quad \text{and} \quad A = \{x : s(x) = -x\}$$ are subrepresentations. The quotient maps $V \otimes V \to \Sym^2 V$ and $V \otimes V \to \bigwedge^2 V$ of Definitions [9.10.3](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#definition-9-10-3) and [9.10.4](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#definition-9-10-4) restrict to isomorphisms $S \cong \Sym^2 V$ and $A \cong \bigwedge^2 V$: the first map kills exactly the span of the tensors $x - s(x)$, which is $A$, and the second kills exactly the span of the tensors $v \otimes v$, which is $S$, because $v \otimes w + w \otimes v = (v + w) \otimes (v + w) - v \otimes v - w \otimes w$.

*Step 1: $\nu(V) = \dim S^G - \dim A^G$.* Fix $g \in G$ and a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$ consisting of eigenvectors of $g$ (Lemma [13.1.5](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#lemma-13-1-5)), with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$. Then $S$ has the basis $e_i \otimes e_j + e_j \otimes e_i$ ($i \leq j$) and $A$ has the basis $e_i \otimes e_j - e_j \otimes e_i$ ($i < j$), and each of these vectors is an eigenvector of $g$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_i \lambda_j$. Hence $$\chi_S(g) - \chi_A(g) = \sum_{i \leq j} \lambda_i \lambda_j - \sum_{i < j} \lambda_i \lambda_j = \sum_i \lambda_i^2 = \chi_V(g^2).$$ Averaging over $G$ and using $\dim X^G = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_g \chi_X(g)$ (Proposition [13.5.1](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-1)) gives Step 1.

*Step 2: invariant forms.* A bilinear form $B$ on $V$ is the same as a linear functional $\beta$ on $V \otimes V$, via $\beta(v \otimes w) = B(v, w)$ (Theorem [9.8.6](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#theorem-9-8-6)). The form $B$ is $G$-invariant if and only if $\beta(gx) = \beta(x)$ for all $g$ and $x$, that is, if and only if $\beta$ is a $G$-invariant element of the dual representation $(V \otimes V)^*$. The form $B$ is symmetric if and only if $\beta \circ s = \beta$, that is, $\beta$ vanishes on $A$; and $B$ is skew-symmetric if and only if $\beta$ vanishes on $S$. Since $V \otimes V = S \oplus A$, restriction to $S$ identifies the symmetric forms with $S^*$, and restriction to $A$ identifies the skew-symmetric forms with $A^*$, compatibly with the actions of $G$. Since $\chi_{S^*} = \ol{\chi_S}$, $$\dim (S^*)^G = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \ol{\chi_S(g)} = \ol{\dim S^G} = \dim S^G,$$ and likewise $\dim (A^*)^G = \dim A^G$. So $\nu(V) = s_+ - s_-$, where $s_+$ is the dimension of the space of $G$-invariant symmetric bilinear forms on $V$ and $s_-$ that of the space of $G$-invariant skew-symmetric ones.

*Step 3.* By Theorem [16.5.4](/notes/math-55a/16-5-quaternionic-representations#theorem-16-5-4): if $\chi_V$ is not real-valued, $s_+ = s_- = 0$ and $\nu(V) = 0$. If $V$ is real, the invariant forms are the multiples of one symmetric form, so $s_+ = 1$, $s_- = 0$, and $\nu(V) = 1$. If $V$ is quaternionic, they are the multiples of one skew-symmetric form, so $s_+ = 0$, $s_- = 1$, and $\nu(V) = -1$.
:::

To compute $\nu(V)$ from a character table, one needs to know, for each conjugacy class, the class of the squares of its elements.
